claims.text: When one or more of the dimensions of a prism or cylinder is multiplied by a constant, its surface area and volume change.
claims.quote: When one or more of the dimensions of a prism or cylinder is multiplied by a constant, the surface area and volume will change.

claims.text: The new surface area and volume of a prism or cylinder whose dimensions have been multiplied by a constant are calculated by using the surface area and volume formulae from the preceding section.
claims.quote: The new surface area and volume can be calculated by using the formulae from the preceding section.

claims.text: There is a relationship between the change in dimensions and the resulting change in surface area and volume.
claims.quote: It is possible to see a relationship between the change in dimensions and the resulting change in surface area and volume.

claims.text: These relationships are used to calculate the new volume or surface area of an object more simply when its dimensions are scaled up or down.
claims.quote: These relationships make it simpler to calculate the new volume or surface area of an object when its dimensions are scaled up or down.

claims.text: The dimensions of a rectangular prism are written l, b and h.
claims.quote: Consider a rectangular prism of dimensions $l$ , $b$ and $h$ .

claims.text: To see the effect of scaling, multiply one, two and then three of the dimensions of the rectangular prism by a constant factor (here 5) and calculate the new volume and surface area each time.
claims.quote: Below we multiply one, two and three of its dimensions by a constant factor of $\text{5}$ and calculate the new volume and surface area.

claims.text: The volume of a rectangular prism with dimensions l, b and h is V = l × b × h = lbh.
The surface area of a rectangular prism with dimensions l, b and h is A = 2[(l × h) + (l × b) + (b × h)] = 2(lh + lb + bh).
When one dimension of a rectangular prism (the height) is multiplied by 5, the new volume is V1 = l × b × 5h = 5(lbh) = 5V.
When one dimension of a rectangular prism (the height) is multiplied by 5, the new surface area is A1 = 2[(l × 5h) + (l × b) + (b × 5h)] = 2(5lh + lb + 5bh).
When two dimensions of a rectangular prism (l and h) are multiplied by 5, the new volume is V2 = 5l × b × 5h = 5.5(lbh) = 5^2 × V.
When two dimensions of a rectangular prism (l and h) are multiplied by 5, the new surface area is A2 = 2[(5l × 5h) + (5l × b) + (b × 5h)] = 2 × 5(5lh + lb + bh).
When all three dimensions of a rectangular prism are multiplied by 5, the new volume is V3 = 5l × 5b × 5h = 5^3(lbh) = 5^3 V.
When all three dimensions of a rectangular prism are multiplied by 5, the new surface area is A3 = 2(5^2 lh + 5^2 lb + 5^2 bh) = 5^2 × 2(lh + lb + bh) = 5^2 A.
When all three dimensions of a rectangular prism are multiplied by a factor k, the new volume is V_k = kl × kb × kh = k^3(lbh) = k^3 V; volume is multiplied by k^3.

When all three dimensions of a rectangular prism are multiplied by a factor k, the new surface area is A_k = 2[(kl × kh) + (kl × kb) + (kb × kh)] = k^2 × 2(lh + lb + bh) = k^2 A; surface area is multiplied by k^2.
The new surface area is written A_n and the new volume is written V_n.
claims.quote: Calculate the new surface area ( ${A}_{n}$ ) and volume ( ${V}_{n}$ )

claims.text: To express the new surface area and volume as a factor of the original, first calculate the original volume and surface area, then the new volume and surface area, then compare the new values with the original ones.
claims.quote: Express the new surface area and volume as a factor of the original surface area and volume.

claims.text: Step 1: the original volume of the prism with base lengths 3 cm and height 4 cm is V = l × b × h = 3 × 3 × 4 = 36 cm^3.
Step 1: the original surface area of the prism is A = 2[(l × h) + (l × b) + (b × h)] = 2[(3 × 4) + (3 × 3) + (3 × 4)] = 66 cm^2.
Step 2: multiplying both base lengths by 3 means two of the dimensions are multiplied by a factor of 3.
claims.quote: Two of the dimensions are multiplied by a factor of 3.

claims.text: Step 2: the new volume is V_n = 3l × 3b × h = 3(3) × 3(3) × 4 = 324 cm^3.
Step 3: to express the new volume as a factor of the original, divide V_n by V: V_n / V = 324 / 36 = 9, so V_n = 9V = 3^2 V.
Step 3: to express the new surface area as a factor of the original, divide A_n by A: A_n / A = 306 / 66, so A_n = (306/66)A = (51/11)A.
To prove the effect of multiplying the height by k, write the new dimensions of the prism as l, b and kh.
claims.quote: The new dimensions are $l$ , $b$ , and $kh$ and so the new volume is:

claims.text: With the height multiplied by k, the new volume is V_n = l × b × (kh) = k(lbh) = kV.
If the height of a rectangular prism is multiplied by a constant k, then the volume also increases by a factor of k.
claims.quote: If the height of a rectangular prism is multiplied by a constant $k$ , then the volume also increases by a factor of $k$ .

claims.text: In this example the volume of a cylinder with radius r and height h is V = πr^2 × h.
In this example the surface area of the cylinder is given as A = πr^2 + 2πrh.
When the radius of the cylinder is multiplied by k, the new dimensions are kr and h.
When the radius of a cylinder is multiplied by k, the new volume is V_n = π(kr)^2 × h = πk^2 r^2 × h = k^2 × πr^2 h = k^2 V.
When the radius of a cylinder is multiplied by k, the new surface area is A_n = π(kr)^2 + 2π(kr)h = πk^2 r^2 + 2πkrh = k^2(πr^2) + k(2πrh).

items.stem: Consider a rectangular prism with a height of $\text{4}$ $\text{cm}$ and base lengths of $\text{3}$ $\text{cm}$ . [figure] Calculate the surface area and volume. Calculate the new surface area ( ${A}_{n}$ ) and volume ( ${V}_{n}$ ) if the base lengths are multiplied by a constant factor of $\text{3}$ . Express the new surface area and volume as a factor of the original surface area and volume.
solution: Calculate the original volume and surface area: $\begin{align*}V&=l\timesb\timesh\\&=3\times3\times4\\&=36\text{cm}^{3}\\\\A&=2\left[(l\timesh)+(l\timesb)+(b\timesh)\right]\\&=2\left[(3\times4)+(3\times3)+(3\times4)\right]\\&=66\text{cm}^{2}\end{align*}$

Calculate the new volume and surface area: Two of the dimensions are multiplied by a factor of 3. $\begin{align*}V_{n}&=3l\times3b\timesh\\&=3(3)\times3(3)\times4\\&=324\text{cm}^{3}\\\\A_{n}&=2\left[(3l\timesh)+(3l\times3b)+(3b\timesh)\right]\\&=2\left[(3(3)\times4)+(3(3)\times3(3))+(3(3)\times4)\right]\\&=306\text{cm}^{2}\end{align*}$

Express the new dimensions as a factor of the original dimensions: $\begin{align*}V&=36\\{V}_{n}&=324\\\frac{{V}_{n}}{V}&=\frac{324}{36}\\&=9\\\therefore{V}_{n}&=9V\\&={3}^{2}V\\\\A&=66\\{A}_{n}&=306\\\frac{{A}_{n}}{A}&=\frac{306}{66}\\\therefore{A}_{n}&=\frac{306}{66}A\\&=\frac{51}{11}A\end{align*}$
items.blind_answer: Original: $A = 66\ \text{cm}^2$, $V = 36\ \text{cm}^3$. New (base 9 by 9, height 4): $A_n = 306\ \text{cm}^2$, $V_n = 324\ \text{cm}^3$. $V_n = 9V$; $A_n = \frac{51}{11}A \approx 4.64A$ (surface area does not change by a constant factor)

items.stem: Consider a cylinder with a radius of $r$ and a height of $h$ . Calculate the new volume and surface area (expressed in terms of $r$ and $h$ ) if the radius is multiplied by a constant factor of $k$ . [figure]
solution: Calculate the original volume and surface area: $\begin{align*}V&=\pi{r}^{2}\timesh\\A&=\pi{r}^{2}+2\pirh\end{align*}$

Calculate the new volume and surface area: The new dimensions are $kr$ and $h$ . $\begin{align*}{V}_{n}&=\pi{\left(kr\right)}^{2}\times h\\&=\pi{k}^{2}{r}^{2}\times h\\&={k}^{2}\times\pi{r}^{2}h\\&={k}^{2}V\\\\{A}_{n}&=\pi{\left(kr\right)}^{2}+2\pi\left(kr\right)h\\&=\pi{k}^{2}{r}^{2}+2\pi krh\\&={k}^{2}\left(\pi{r}^{2}\right)+k\left(2\pi rh\right)\end{align*}$
items.blind_answer: $V_n = k^2\pi r^2 h$ and $A_n = 2\pi k^2 r^2 + 2\pi k r h = 2\pi k r\,(kr + h)$

items.stem: If the length of the radius of a circle is a third of its original size, what will the area of the new circle be? [figure]
solution: The area of the original circle is: $\pir^{2}$ . Now we reduce the radius by a third. In other words we multiply $r$ by one third. The new area is:
$\begin{align*}A_{\text{new}}&=\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}r\right)^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{9}\pir^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{9}A\end{align*}$
Therefore, if the radius of a circle is a third of its original size, the area of the new circle will be $\frac{1}{9}$ the original area.

items.stem: If the length of the base's radius and height of a cone is doubled, what will the surface area of the new cone be? [figure]
solution: We can find the new area by noting that the area will change by a factor of $k$ when we change the dimensions of the cone. In this case we are changing two dimensions of the cone and so the new area will be: $A_{\text{new}}=k^{2}A$ The value of $k$ comes from the word “doubled” in the question: the value of $k$ is 2. So the new area of the cone will be $A_{\text{new}}=4\times A$ if we double the height and the base's radius of the cone. Therefore the surface area of the new cone will be 4 times the original surface area.

items.stem: If the height of a prism is doubled, how much will its volume increase by?
solution: We do not know if we have a rectangular prism or a triangular prism. However we do know that the volume of a prism is given by:
$V=\text{area of base}\times\text{height of prism}$
Now we are changing just one dimension of the prism: the height. Therefore the new volume is given by:
$\begin{align*}V_{\text{new}}&=\text{areaofbase}\times2(\text{heightofprism})\\&=2V\end{align*}$
Therefore the volume of the prism doubles if the height is doubled.

solution: When we multiply the sides of a square by a factor of $k$ the area of the square will increase by $k^{2}$ . In this case we are making each side of the square a quarter of the original size so we get:
$\begin{align*}A_{\text{new}}&=\left(\frac{1}{4}s\right)^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{16}s^{2}\\&=\frac{1}{16}A\end{align*}$
Therefore, if each side of a square is a quarter of its original size, the area of the new square will be $\frac{1}{16}$ times the original square's area.
